query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of reactive elements (e.g., Yttrium and Hafnium) during melting will improve the high-temperature and corrosive environment stability of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without sacrificing its strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a fine lamellar microstructure with coupled fcc and B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce low concentrations of Y and Hf into the alloy during casting (i.e. microalloying) to modify interfacial properties and oxide scale formation.
generation.conditions: Alloy is processed under conventional casting/thermo-mechanical processing conditions; performance is evaluated under extreme temperature fluctuations, subjected to long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep tests), and in corrosive environments (e.g., molten salt exposure).
generation.structural_mediator: The dopants are expected to segregate at phase boundaries and grain boundaries to promote the formation of more adherent and stable oxide layers, refine the lamellar architecture slightly, and possibly encourage controlled secondary precipitation (e.g., fine L12) that strengthens interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Y and Hf act as reactive elements that improve oxide scale adhesion and inhibit spallation under thermal cycling, while their presence at grain boundaries assists in stabilizing the microstructure under creep loading. These changes mitigate degradation from mechanical loading and harsh environments without degrading the intrinsic strength–ductility synergy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The doped alloy should exhibit enhanced resistance to thermal fluctuations, lower creep rates at room temperature, and improved corrosion performance (lower oxide spallation and degradation), all while retaining an excellent balance of strength and ductility compared to the undoped alloy.
generation.baseline: The conventional AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy offers high tensile strength and ductility but currently shows limitations in long-term creep behavior, thermal stability under extreme temperature cycles, and corrosion resistance.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be beneficial when dopant levels are carefully optimized; excessive addition might lead to brittle intermetallic phase formation or unwanted microstructural changes. Its effectiveness is assumed only under conditions similar to those used in conventional casting and subsequent processing.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal concentrations and distribution of Y and Hf that maximize performance improvements without compromising mechanical properties remain to be determined. Effects on the precipitation behavior and interface stability under different thermal/mechanical environments require further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of samples: one set of standard as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA and a second set doped with low levels of Y and Hf. Subject both groups to a series of rigorous tests that simulate extreme temperature cycling, long-term mechanical loading (including standardized room-temperature creep tests), and corrosive environments (e.g., exposure to molten Na2SO4/NaCl mixtures). Use microscopy (TEM, SEM) and diffraction (XRD) to analyze microstructural stability pre- and post-tests.
measurements: Tensile properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation)
Creep rate measurements under constant load at room temperature
Corrosion performance (area/degree of oxide spallation, weight loss)
Microstructural evaluation (phase stability, grain boundary behavior, precipitate distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-Hf doped samples do not demonstrate statistically significant enhancements in high-temperature stability, reduced creep rates, and improved corrosion resistance relative to the control samples—or if they show a detrimental impact on strength or ductility—the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractBoth crack-free AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and Y and Hf co-doping AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA (YHf-EHEA) coatings were prepared by laser cladding. The solidification microstructure, thermal stability, and hot corrosion performance of the coatings at 900 °C under 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts were investigated. The experimental results showed that the structure of the as-deposited coatings consisted of FCC and BCC/B2 phases. After heat treatment, an Al-rich L12 phase was precipitated in the FCC phase of all coatings. The grain sizes of the EHEA and YHf-EHEA coatings after heat treatment at 900 °C for 10 h increased by 27.5% and 15.7%, respectively, compared to the as-deposited coatings. Meanwhile, after hot corrosion, the spallation areas of the YHf-EHEA and EHEA coatings accounted for 14.98% and 5.67% of the total surface area, respectively.
